title: Psychotropic Medication Dosage Calculator
problem: PMHNPs spend significant time calculating medication dosages, especially for titration schedules, weight-based dosing, and cross-tapering between psychotropic medications. Errors in dosage calculations can lead to adverse drug reactions, serotonin syndrome, or therapeutic failure. Manual calculations during busy 15-patient days increase the risk of prescribing errors.
who: All PMHNPs prescribing psychotropic medications, especially new graduates

skill_spec.name: Psychotropic Dosage & Titration Calculator
skill_spec.one_liner: Calculates medication dosages, titration schedules, and cross-taper plans for common psychotropic medications
skill_spec.formula_hint: Weight-based: dose_mg = weight_kg * mg_per_kg_rate. Titration: increment by 25-50% of starting dose per interval. Geriatric: start at 50% of adult dose. Renal adjustment per GFR ranges.

What's the cross-taper plan switching from Lexapro 20mg to Effexor XR 150mg?

title: Psychiatric Billing & CPT Code Calculator
problem: PMHNPs struggle with selecting correct CPT codes for psychiatric evaluations, psychotherapy add-ons, and medication management visits. Incorrect coding leads to claim denials, lost revenue, and audit risk. Combining E/M codes with psychotherapy add-on codes (90833/90836/90838) and knowing when to use 90792 vs 99213-99215 is confusing, especially for those in private practice.
who: PMHNPs in private practice and those billing independently

skill_spec.name: Psychiatric CPT Code & Reimbursement Calculator
skill_spec.one_liner: Selects correct CPT codes for psychiatric visits and calculates expected reimbursement
skill_spec.formula_hint: Initial psych eval = 90792. Follow-up E/M by MDM complexity: low=99213, moderate=99214, high=99215. Therapy add-ons: 16-37min=90833, 38-52min=90836, 53+min=90838. Medicare rates from CMS fee schedule. Telehealth modifier 95.

title: Prior Authorization for Psychiatric Medications
problem: PMHNPs spend hours weekly on prior authorization (PA) forms for psychotropic medications, especially atypical antipsychotics, brand-name SSRIs/SNRIs, stimulants, and newer agents like Spravato. Each insurer has different PA requirements, and missing criteria leads to denials and treatment delays for patients who may be in crisis.
who: All prescribing PMHNPs, especially in outpatient settings

skill_spec.name: Psychiatric Prior Authorization Guide
skill_spec.one_liner: Step-by-step checklist for completing prior authorizations for common psychotropic medications with payer-specific criteria
steps: Step 1: Verify the medication requires PA - check formulary status on payer portal
Step 2: Document clinical justification - diagnosis (ICD-10), symptom severity scores (PHQ-9/GAD-7), treatment history
Step 3: Document step therapy failures - list prior medications tried, doses, duration, and reason for discontinuation
Step 4: Include lab results if applicable (metabolic panel for antipsychotics, thyroid for lithium, drug levels)
Step 5: Complete payer-specific PA form - attach clinical notes supporting medical necessity
Step 6: Submit via CoverMyMeds, Surescripts, or payer portal
Step 7: Track submission - set 72-hour follow-up reminder
Step 8: If denied - review denial reason, file peer-to-peer review request within appeal window
Step 9: Document all PA activity in patient chart for continuity
warnings: Warning: Controlled substances (Schedule II stimulants) may require additional DEA documentation
Warning: Some states require PA decisions within 24-72 hours - know your state's prompt PA law
Warning: Spravato (esketamine) requires REMS certification documentation
regulatory_refs: Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act

example_queries: Walk me through the prior auth process for Vraylar for a patient who failed two SSRIs

title: Suicide Risk Assessment Documentation
problem: PMHNPs must conduct and document thorough suicide risk assessments using evidence-based tools (Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale, PHQ-9 Item 9). Inadequate documentation is the leading cause of malpractice claims in psychiatry. Under time pressure with 15 patients per day, critical assessment elements may be missed, creating both patient safety and legal exposure risks.
who: All PMHNPs, especially those treating depression, PTSD, and substance use disorders

skill_spec.name: Suicide Risk Assessment & Safety Plan Checklist
skill_spec.one_liner: Comprehensive suicide risk assessment checklist with documentation requirements and safety planning steps
steps: Step 1: Screen with validated tool - PHQ-9 Item 9 or ASQ (Ask Suicide Screening Questions)
Step 2: If positive screen - administer Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS)
Step 3: Assess risk factors - prior attempts, family history, access to lethal means, substance use, recent losses
Step 4: Assess protective factors - social support, reasons for living, engagement in treatment, religious beliefs
Step 5: Determine risk level - low/moderate/high/imminent based on structured assessment
Step 6: Document clinical decision-making rationale for level of care determination
Step 7: For moderate+ risk - create collaborative Safety Plan (Stanley-Brown template)
Step 8: Address means restriction - document lethal means counseling conversation
Step 9: Establish follow-up plan - timing, method, emergency contacts
Step 10: If imminent risk - initiate involuntary hold procedures per state law (Baker Act/5150 equivalent)
Step 11: Document all elements in EHR with time-stamped entries
warnings: Warning: Never use 'no-suicide contracts' - they are not evidence-based and provide no legal protection
Warning: Document why you did NOT hospitalize moderate-risk patients - this is the most litigated decision
Warning: State involuntary commitment laws vary - know your state's criteria and time limits
regulatory_refs: State Baker Act / involuntary commitment statutes
42 CFR Part 2 for substance use patients

example_queries: Walk me through a complete suicide risk assessment for a patient with passive SI
What must I document when I decide NOT to hospitalize a patient with suicidal ideation?
How do I create a Stanley-Brown Safety Plan with my patient?

title: Psychiatric Progress Note Generator (SOAP)
problem: PMHNPs spend 1-2 hours daily on documentation, writing SOAP-format progress notes for each of their 15 daily patients. Notes must capture mental status exam findings, medication changes with rationale, risk assessments, and treatment plan updates. Poor notes increase malpractice risk and lead to claim denials. Many PMHNPs document after hours, contributing to burnout.
who: All PMHNPs, especially those in high-volume outpatient settings

skill_spec.name: Psychiatric SOAP Note Generator
skill_spec.one_liner: Generates structured psychiatric progress notes in SOAP format with medication management and risk assessment sections
skill_spec.structure_hint: Subjective (chief complaint, self-report, medication adherence, side effects) -> Objective (MSE: appearance, behavior, speech, mood, affect, thought process, thought content, cognition, insight, judgment; vitals if applicable; screening scores) -> Assessment (diagnoses with ICD-10, clinical formulation, risk assessment) -> Plan (medication changes with rationale, therapy plan, labs ordered, follow-up timing, safety plan if applicable)

title: Drug Interaction Checker for Psychotropics
problem: Psychiatric polypharmacy is common - many patients take 3+ psychotropic medications plus medical medications. PMHNPs must check for dangerous interactions like serotonin syndrome (SSRI + tramadol), QTc prolongation (multiple antipsychotics), and metabolic interactions (CYP450 inhibitors/inducers). While e-prescribing alerts exist, they generate excessive alerts causing 'alert fatigue', and many critical psychiatric-specific interactions are missed.
who: All prescribing PMHNPs, especially those managing complex cases

skill_spec.name: Psychotropic Drug Interaction Analyzer
skill_spec.one_liner: Analyzes psychotropic medication combinations for dangerous interactions including serotonin syndrome risk, QTc prolongation, and CYP450 conflicts

inputs.name: medications
inputs.label: List of all current medications with doses

skill_spec.formula_hint: Serotonin risk: count serotonergic agents (SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans, tramadol, MAOIs, St. John's Wort). QTc risk: sum individual drug QTc-prolonging potentials. CYP450: check 2D6, 3A4, 2C19 inhibitor/inducer status of each drug.

example_queries: Check interactions between Prozac 40mg, Trazodone 100mg, and Abilify 10mg
Is it safe to add Wellbutrin to a patient already on Adderall and Lexapro?
Serotonin syndrome risk if I add Tramadol to a patient on Cymbalta 60mg?

title: Controlled Substance Prescribing Compliance
problem: PMHNPs prescribing Schedule II-V controlled substances (stimulants, benzodiazepines, Suboxone) must navigate DEA regulations, state PDMP check requirements, prescription limits, and documentation requirements. Rules vary by state - some require PDMP checks before every controlled substance prescription, others every 90 days. Non-compliance can result in DEA license revocation and criminal charges.
who: All PMHNPs with DEA registration, especially those prescribing stimulants and benzodiazepines

skill_spec.name: Controlled Substance Prescribing Compliance Checklist
skill_spec.one_liner: Step-by-step compliance checklist for prescribing controlled substances including PDMP, DEA, and state-specific requirements
steps: Step 1: Verify your DEA registration is active and covers the schedule of the drug being prescribed
Step 2: Check state PDMP before prescribing - document results in patient chart
Step 3: Verify patient identity and confirm informed consent for controlled substance treatment
Step 4: Document clinical indication with ICD-10 diagnosis supporting the prescription
Step 5: For Schedule II (stimulants, some opioids): no refills permitted, new Rx required each time, max 90-day supply in most states
Step 6: For benzodiazepines: document risk-benefit analysis, consider benzodiazepine use disorder screening
Step 7: For buprenorphine/Suboxone: verify X-waiver no longer required post-2023, but document MAT training completion
Step 8: Conduct and document urine drug screen (UDS) per practice protocol (typically every 3-6 months for chronic CS)
Step 9: Review and sign controlled substance agreement/treatment contract with patient
Step 10: E-prescribe via EPCS-certified system (mandatory in most states for Schedule II)
Step 11: Set follow-up appointment within state-mandated interval for continued prescribing
warnings: Warning: PDMP check requirements vary by state - some require checks before EVERY controlled substance Rx
Warning: Prescribing controlled substances via telehealth has federal and state restrictions post-COVID PHE
Warning: Co-prescribing benzodiazepines and opioids requires FDA black box warning documentation
regulatory_refs: Ryan Haight Online Pharmacy Consumer Protection Act

example_queries: What are the PDMP check requirements for prescribing Adderall in California?
Can I prescribe Xanax via telehealth to a patient in another state?
What documentation do I need for continuing a patient on Suboxone?

title: PMHNP Credential & License Renewal Tracker
problem: PMHNPs must maintain multiple credentials with different renewal cycles: state nursing license (1-2 years), ANCC board certification (every 5 years requiring 75 CE hours + pharmacology hours), DEA license (every 3 years), collaborative practice agreements (state-dependent), malpractice insurance, and NPI. Missing a renewal deadline can mean inability to practice and prescribe, losing income and patient access.

title: Involuntary Psychiatric Hold Procedures by State
problem: When a patient presents with imminent danger to self or others, PMHNPs must initiate involuntary psychiatric holds. Every state has different laws (Baker Act in Florida, 5150 in California, etc.) with different criteria, time limits, required documentation, and procedures. Making an error - either failing to hold a dangerous patient or improperly detaining one - carries enormous legal and safety consequences. In crisis moments, PMHNPs need immediate access to their state's specific requirements.
who: All PMHNPs, especially those in emergency, inpatient, and crisis settings

title: Treatment Plan Generator
problem: PMHNPs must create comprehensive treatment plans for every patient, typically reviewed every 90 days. Plans must include DSM-5 diagnoses, measurable goals, treatment modalities, medication rationale, and expected outcomes. Insurance companies and accreditation bodies (Joint Commission) audit treatment plans for compliance. Creating individualized, standards-compliant plans for 15 patients is time-consuming and often done after hours.
who: All PMHNPs, especially in outpatient and community mental health settings

skill_spec.name: Psychiatric Treatment Plan Generator
skill_spec.one_liner: Generates individualized psychiatric treatment plans with measurable goals, interventions, and review timelines
skill_spec.structure_hint: Patient demographics -> DSM-5 diagnoses (primary and comorbid) -> Problem list with baseline measures (PHQ-9, GAD-7 scores) -> SMART goals (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) -> Interventions (medication management, psychotherapy type, frequency) -> Crisis plan -> Discharge criteria -> Review timeline (90 days) -> Patient/provider signatures

title: Psychiatric Medication Side Effect & Monitoring Guide
problem: Each class of psychotropic medication requires specific monitoring - metabolic panels for antipsychotics (metabolic syndrome risk), lithium levels and thyroid/renal function for mood stabilizers, liver function for valproate, CBC for clozapine (REMS program). PMHNPs must remember which labs to order, at what intervals, and what values require intervention. Missing monitoring can result in serious adverse events and malpractice liability.
who: All prescribing PMHNPs, especially those managing antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, and clozapine

title: Scope of Practice by State Advisor
problem: PMHNP scope of practice varies dramatically across states - 28 states + DC allow full practice authority while others require physician collaboration or supervision. Rules differ for prescriptive authority (especially controlled substances), practice agreements, and telehealth across state lines. With the Nurse Licensure Compact and expanding full practice authority (California SB 1451 in 2026), the landscape is constantly changing. PMHNPs expanding into telehealth or relocating need current state-specific guidance.
who: PMHNPs considering multi-state practice, telehealth expansion, or relocation

title: Private Practice Startup Financial Calculator
problem: Many experienced PMHNPs want to open private practices but struggle with financial projections. They need to calculate startup costs, monthly overhead, required patient volume to break even, insurance vs cash-pay revenue modeling, and tax obligations as a business owner. Poor financial planning leads to practice failure or unsustainable patient loads.
who: PMHNPs transitioning to private practice ownership

skill_spec.name: PMHNP Private Practice Financial Calculator
skill_spec.one_liner: Calculates startup costs, monthly overhead, break-even patient volume, and revenue projections for a PMHNP private practice
skill_spec.formula_hint: Revenue = patients_per_day * days_per_week * 4.33 * avg_rate * collection_rate(~85% insurance, 98% cash). Overhead = rent + EHR + malpractice($3K-6K/yr) + billing(5-8% revenue) + licensing + CE + phone/internet. Self-employment tax = 15.3% on net. Break-even = monthly_overhead / avg_net_per_visit.
